cues.text: St. James in Spain

According to a tradition long cherished in Spain, the Apostle St. James the Greater traveled to the Iberian Peninsula in the years after Pentecost to preach the Gospel, becoming, in this account, the first evangelizer of what is now Spain.

Preaching along the banks of the Ebro River at the Roman city of Caesaraugusta — modern Zaragoza — James is said to have met with little success and few converts, leaving him discouraged in his mission.
The tradition holds that it was at this low point, while James prayed with a handful of disciples, that Our Lady is said to have appeared to him.
The Apparition on the Pillar
Tradition dates the apparition to the night of January 2 in the year 40.

James is said to have beheld the Virgin Mary — while she was still living in Jerusalem, making this uniquely an apparition granted during her earthly life — standing atop a pillar of jasper, surrounded by angels.
Our Lady is said to have encouraged James in his mission, assuring him that though his labors seemed to bear little fruit, the Christian faith would flourish abundantly in Spain.
She asked that a chapel be built on the site in her honor, with the pillar as the base of its altar, promising that through it God would work wonders for those who sought her intercession there.
The First Marian Shrine
James and his companions are said to have built a small chapel beside the Ebro.
Traditionally, it is honored as the first church in the world raised in honor of the Virgin Mary—and, uniquely among Marian shrines, established during her own lifetime.
James subsequently returned to Jerusalem, where he was beheaded by Herod Agrippa I around AD 44, becoming the first Apostle to be martyred.
Over the centuries, a succession of larger churches replaced the original chapel.
The present Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar was largely built between the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and decorated in part by Francisco de Goya.
It still houses the venerated pillar and a statue of Mary above it.
Approval and Devotion
As one of the oldest Marian traditions in Christendom, devotion to Our Lady of the Pillar received favor from a succession of popes across the centuries.

They extended indulgences and liturgical honors to the shrine and its observance, though the precise record of which pontiffs acted, and when, is a matter for further documentary verification rather than settled here.
Because the tradition rests on ancient local memory rather than a documented modern investigation, the Church treats it as pious, long-received tradition.
Like other apparitions of the apostolic era, it is not a formally "approved" apparition in the modern canonical sense.
Our Lady of the Pillar is honored as patroness of Spain, of the Hispanic peoples, and of the Spanish Civil Guard; her feast, October 12, coincides with Spain's national day.
Legacy
During the Spanish Civil War in 1936, three aerial bombs struck the basilica but reportedly failed to explode — an episode still recounted by pilgrims and displayed within the shrine.

The Basilica of the Pilar remains one of the great pilgrimage destinations of Spain, standing alongside the Camino de Santiago as an expression of the enduring bond between St. James, the Spanish people, and devotion to the Mother of God.
